questions.question: A 65-year-old patient with a history of diabetes mellitus and coronary artery disease presents with dizziness and near syncope. ECG shows a wide-complex bradyarrhythmia. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Symptomatic bradycardia with signs of poor perfusion (near-syncope) refractory to atropine requires transcutaneous pacing per ACLS bradycardia algorithm.

explanations.A: Amiodarone treats tachyarrhythmias, not symptomatic bradyarrhythmia; it can worsen bradycardia.
explanations.B: Symptomatic bradycardia with signs of poor perfusion (near-syncope) refractory to atropine requires transcutaneous pacing per ACLS bradycardia algorithm.
explanations.C: Anticoagulants do not correct the underlying rhythm problem; observation alone is unsafe in symptomatic bradycardia.
explanations.D: Atropine is first-line for symptomatic bradycardia but is ineffective in high-degree AV blocks with wide QRS; pacing is then indicated.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: Identify the type of anesthesia shown in the image (needle placed in the epidural space, catheter threaded, LOR-to-saline technique).
questions.explanation: The Tuohy needle, loss-of-resistance technique, and catheter shown are classic features of epidural anesthesia.

explanations.A: Subdural block is an accidental placement, not an intentional technique demonstrated here.
explanations.B: Spinal anesthesia uses a smaller-gauge needle placed through the dura into CSF; no catheter is threaded.
explanations.C: The Tuohy needle, loss-of-resistance technique, and catheter shown are classic features of epidural anesthesia.
explanations.D: General anesthesia is delivered via inhalational/IV agents and airway devices, not a spinal needle.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A case of road traffic accident (RTA) develops neuropathic pain. Which drug is most appropriate for the management of neuropathic pain?
questions.explanation: Gabapentin (a gabapentinoid) is first-line for neuropathic pain along with pregabalin, TCAs and SNRIs.

explanations.A: Acetaminophen treats mild nociceptive pain, not neuropathic pain (no central anticonvulsant action).
explanations.B: NSAIDs act on inflammatory nociceptive pain; they are ineffective for neuropathic pain.
explanations.C: Tramadol is a weak opioid with modest SNRI activity — used as adjunct, not first-line.
explanations.D: Gabapentin (a gabapentinoid) is first-line for neuropathic pain along with pregabalin, TCAs and SNRIs.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has a history of gastric ulcer. Which drug is most appropriate for this patient?
questions.explanation: Celecoxib is a COX-2 selective inhibitor with lower GI ulcer risk — preferred in RA patients with PUD history.

explanations.A: Celecoxib is a COX-2 selective inhibitor with lower GI ulcer risk — preferred in RA patients with PUD history.
explanations.B: Naloxone is an opioid antagonist; it has no anti-inflammatory role.
explanations.C: Paracetamol has minimal anti-inflammatory effect; inadequate for RA disease control.
explanations.D: Ibuprofen is a non-selective NSAID and significantly increases ulcer/bleeding risk.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT typically seen in a patient with heat stroke?
questions.explanation: Classic (non-exertional) heat stroke shows anhidrosis — sweating fails due to thermoregulatory collapse.

explanations.A: Classic (non-exertional) heat stroke shows anhidrosis — sweating fails due to thermoregulatory collapse.
explanations.B: Core temperature >40°C (≈104°F) is a hallmark; 103°F (39.4°C) is consistent.
explanations.C: Tachycardia is typical as the body tries to dissipate heat.
explanations.D: Hot, dry, flushed skin is the classic presentation due to failed sweating.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A patient on ECMO continues to have difficulty breathing despite adequate settings. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Persistent respiratory distress despite adequate settings mandates ruling out circuit issues (kinks, thrombus, cannula malposition) first.

explanations.A: Increasing tidal volume risks ventilator-induced lung injury and ignores the actual problem.
explanations.B: Persistent respiratory distress despite adequate settings mandates ruling out circuit issues (kinks, thrombus, cannula malposition) first.
explanations.C: Blindly escalating flow can worsen hemolysis and mask the root cause.
explanations.D: Raising FiO2 to 100% is oxygen toxicity risk and doesn't address a mechanical failure.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: In a patient with a shockable cardiac rhythm, after how many shocks should adrenaline be administered?
questions.explanation: AHA guideline — for VF/pulseless VT, epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO is given after the 3rd shock; repeat every 3–5 minutes.

explanations.A: 0.1 mL is a pediatric dose; in adult ACLS the dose is 1 mg IV.
explanations.B: Correct dose is 1 mg, and timing in shockable rhythms is after the third shock (then every 3–5 min).
explanations.C: AHA guideline — for VF/pulseless VT, epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO is given after the 3rd shock; repeat every 3–5 minutes.
explanations.D: Dose is right (1 mg) but timing is wrong; delayed until the 3rd shock in shockable rhythms.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: Stenosis or obstruction of the Foramina of Luschka and Magendie is most commonly associated with which condition?
questions.explanation: Dandy-Walker malformation = cystic dilation of 4th ventricle + cerebellar vermis hypoplasia due to atresia of Luschka & Magendie.

explanations.A: Dandy-Walker malformation = cystic dilation of 4th ventricle + cerebellar vermis hypoplasia due to atresia of Luschka & Magendie.
explanations.B: Arnold-Chiari involves cerebellar tonsillar herniation, not foraminal atresia.
explanations.C: Aqueductal stenosis obstructs the cerebral aqueduct (between 3rd and 4th ventricles), not the foramina.
explanations.D: Spina bifida is a neural tube defect; unrelated to CSF foraminal atresia.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: Which anti-tuberculosis drug is the most bactericidal?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin is rated the most bactericidal first-line anti-TB drug; it kills actively dividing and semi-dormant bacilli.

explanations.A: Rifampicin is rated the most bactericidal first-line anti-TB drug; it kills actively dividing and semi-dormant bacilli.
explanations.B: Ethambutol is primarily bacteriostatic and used to prevent resistance.
explanations.C: Isoniazid is highly bactericidal against rapidly dividing bacilli (early bactericidal activity) but rifampicin has the broadest bactericidal reach.
explanations.D: Pyrazinamide is a sterilising drug effective in acidic intracellular pH; not the most bactericidal overall.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A patient is prescribed an inhaler with 200 puffs; the order is 2 puffs every 6 hours. For how many days will one inhaler last?
questions.explanation: 2 puffs × 4 doses/day = 8 puffs/day → 200 ÷ 8 = 25 days.

explanations.A: 20 × 8 = 160 puffs — only consumed 160, not 200.
explanations.B: 2 puffs × 4 doses/day = 8 puffs/day → 200 ÷ 8 = 25 days.
explanations.C: 28 × 8 = 224 puffs — exceeds 200.
explanations.D: 30 × 8 = 240 puffs — exceeds 200.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: Calcium gluconate is NOT given by which method?
questions.explanation: Rapid IV push of calcium causes bradycardia, hypotension, cardiac arrest; never given fast IV.

explanations.A: Rapid IV push of calcium causes bradycardia, hypotension, cardiac arrest; never given fast IV.
explanations.B: Slow IV push over 5–10 minutes (diluted) is the standard for acute hyperkalemia/tetany.
explanations.C: IV infusion (diluted in dextrose/saline) over 30–60 minutes is accepted for symptomatic hypocalcemia.
explanations.D: Oral calcium gluconate is available for maintenance therapy.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: What is the recommended breathing rate during CPR in a patient with an advanced airway?
questions.explanation: AHA 2020 — with an advanced airway, give 1 breath every 6 seconds = 10 breaths/min with continuous chest compressions.

explanations.A: AHA 2020 — with an advanced airway, give 1 breath every 6 seconds = 10 breaths/min with continuous chest compressions.
explanations.B: 12 breaths/min is the rescue breathing rate without compressions.
explanations.C: 20/min is used only in pediatric advanced airway (every 2–3 s).
explanations.D: 6/min is a pediatric rescue breathing rate in specific contexts, not adult CPR.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A burn patient requires 4800 mL fluid in the first 24 hours as per the Parkland formula. How much fluid should be given in the first 8 hours?
questions.explanation: Parkland protocol: give half (50%) of calculated 24-hour volume in first 8 hours → 4800 ÷ 2 = 2400 mL.

explanations.A: 1200 mL = 25% — under-resuscitation; Parkland mandates 50% in first 8 hours.
explanations.B: Parkland protocol: give half (50%) of calculated 24-hour volume in first 8 hours → 4800 ÷ 2 = 2400 mL.
explanations.C: 1800 mL is neither ½ nor ¼ of 4800; not part of Parkland pacing.
explanations.D: 3000 mL > 50%; would risk over-resuscitation/compartment syndrome.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: Elevated jugular venous pressure is most commonly caused by:
questions.explanation: Increased intravascular volume elevates right atrial pressure → raised JVP (also seen in RHF, tamponade).

explanations.A: Increased intravascular volume elevates right atrial pressure → raised JVP (also seen in RHF, tamponade).
explanations.B: Fluid overload is a broader term; hypervolemia is the specific hemodynamic cause. Both technically raise JVP, but the exam's intended answer is hypervolemia.
explanations.C: Hypovolemia reduces venous return and lowers JVP.
explanations.D: Dehydration (volume loss) similarly lowers JVP.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A patient receiving heparin has an aPTT of 85 seconds. What is the most appropriate next action?
options: Hold the next dose of heparin
questions.explanation: Therapeutic aPTT on heparin = 1.5–2.5× control (≈46–70 s). 85 s is supra-therapeutic → hold dose and recheck.

explanations.A: Therapeutic aPTT on heparin = 1.5–2.5× control (≈46–70 s). 85 s is supra-therapeutic → hold dose and recheck.
explanations.B: Increasing would worsen bleeding risk.
explanations.C: aPTT is outside therapeutic range; leaving dose unchanged is unsafe.
explanations.D: Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not heparin; heparin reversal uses protamine sulfate.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a bougie during airway management?
options: To assist endotracheal tube placement in a difficult airway
To measure airway resistance during mechanical ventilation
To facilitate suctioning of tracheal secretions
To maintain airway patency during mask ventilation
questions.explanation: Bougie (gum-elastic introducer) is railroaded into the trachea when glottic view is poor, guiding the ETT.

explanations.A: Bougie (gum-elastic introducer) is railroaded into the trachea when glottic view is poor, guiding the ETT.
explanations.B: Airway resistance is measured on the ventilator, not with a bougie.
explanations.C: Suctioning uses a soft/hard suction catheter, not a bougie.
explanations.D: Airway patency during mask ventilation is maintained by oral/nasal airways, not a bougie.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: During central venous catheter (CVC) insertion, a patient develops sudden dyspnea and diminished breath sounds on one side. What is the most likely complication?
questions.explanation: Inadvertent pleural puncture during subclavian/IJ CVC insertion → sudden dyspnea + unilateral diminished breath sounds = pneumothorax.

explanations.A: Inadvertent pleural puncture during subclavian/IJ CVC insertion → sudden dyspnea + unilateral diminished breath sounds = pneumothorax.
explanations.B: Hemothorax presents similarly but with dullness to percussion + shock; less immediate on insertion.
explanations.C: Tamponade (late perforation of RV) causes Beck's triad — muffled heart sounds, hypotension, JVD.
explanations.D: Air embolism causes sudden hypoxia + mill-wheel murmur; bilateral breath sounds usually preserved.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: Which of the following is an EARLY sign of increased intracranial pressure (ICP)?
questions.explanation: Morning headache, vomiting (often projectile, non-bilious), and visual changes are early ICP features.

explanations.A: Bradycardia is part of Cushing's triad — a late, pre-herniation sign.
explanations.B: Irregular (Cheyne-Stokes/ataxic) respiration is a late Cushing triad component.
explanations.C: Morning headache, vomiting (often projectile, non-bilious), and visual changes are early ICP features.
explanations.D: Hypertension with widened pulse pressure is late (Cushing response).

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A COPD patient develops respiratory acidosis. Which intervention is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: BiPAP (NIV) is first-line for COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis — it unloads work of breathing and improves CO2 clearance.

explanations.A: BiPAP (NIV) is first-line for COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis — it unloads work of breathing and improves CO2 clearance.
explanations.B: Invasive ventilation is reserved for NIV failure or contraindication.
explanations.C: Bicarbonate does not treat the underlying hypoventilation and can cause paradoxical CSF acidosis.
explanations.D: Fluid restriction doesn't address respiratory failure.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: During dialysis, a patient's potassium level rises to 6.8 mEq/L. What is the immediate life-saving intervention?
questions.explanation: IV calcium gluconate immediately stabilises myocardial membrane against lethal arrhythmia — first step in life-threatening hyperkalemia.

explanations.A: IV calcium gluconate immediately stabilises myocardial membrane against lethal arrhythmia — first step in life-threatening hyperkalemia.
explanations.B: Dietary restriction is long-term prevention, not acute rescue.
explanations.C: Furosemide requires functioning kidneys; useless in dialysis-dependent anuria.
explanations.D: Fluid restriction doesn't lower serum K+ acutely.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: Atropine is given before abdominal surgery to:
questions.explanation: Atropine is an antimuscarinic — reduces salivary, bronchial and gastric secretions, preventing aspiration during anesthesia.

explanations.A: Atropine is an antimuscarinic — reduces salivary, bronchial and gastric secretions, preventing aspiration during anesthesia.
explanations.B: Atropine decreases peristalsis (paralytic effect on GI smooth muscle).
explanations.C: Atropine has no antimicrobial property.
explanations.D: Atropine causes urinary retention, not diuresis.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A patient presents with pelvic trauma associated with testicular injury. What is the priority nursing action?
options: Apply ice packs and reassurance only
Start antibiotics and send urine culture
questions.explanation: Blood at meatus, scrotal/perineal hematoma → avoid Foley until retrograde urethrogram rules out urethral injury; supra-pubic cystostomy preferred.

explanations.A: Blind catheterization can convert a partial urethral tear into complete disruption.
explanations.B: Blood at meatus, scrotal/perineal hematoma → avoid Foley until retrograde urethrogram rules out urethral injury; supra-pubic cystostomy preferred.
explanations.C: Pain relief alone ignores possible urethral disruption and bladder retention.
explanations.D: Antibiotics and culture are secondary to ruling out urethral injury.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: Which finding in a patient receiving opioid analgesics indicates the most serious concern and requires immediate intervention?
questions.explanation: Respiratory rate <12 signals opioid-induced respiratory depression — life-threatening; prepare naloxone and stimulate patient.

explanations.A: Constipation is common, chronic, and managed with bowel regimen.
explanations.B: Nausea/vomiting is expected and treated with antiemetics.
explanations.C: Respiratory rate <12 signals opioid-induced respiratory depression — life-threatening; prepare naloxone and stimulate patient.
explanations.D: Retention is a side effect but not immediately life-threatening.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A patient on mechanical ventilation shows sudden desaturation and increased peak airway pressure. What is the immediate nursing action?
questions.explanation: Sudden ↑peak pressure + desaturation is typically secretions or kinked tube — suction first (DOPES: Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment, Stacking).

explanations.A: Increasing FiO2 doesn't remove obstruction causing high peak pressures.
explanations.B: Sudden ↑peak pressure + desaturation is typically secretions or kinked tube — suction first (DOPES: Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment, Stacking).
explanations.C: Bronchodilators help if wheeze-driven; addressed after clearing the airway.
explanations.D: Notifying the physician comes after the first-line nursing intervention to rescue the patient.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A patient with a history of peptic ulcer requires pain management. Which analgesic approach is safest?
questions.explanation: Safest approach is to avoid NSAIDs and use acetaminophen or a COX-2 selective with PPI if absolutely required.

explanations.A: NSAIDs directly impair mucosal protection and worsen ulcer.
explanations.B: Safest approach is to avoid NSAIDs and use acetaminophen or a COX-2 selective with PPI if absolutely required.
explanations.C: Aspirin is a potent ulcerogenic agent — contraindicated.
explanations.D: PPI reduces but doesn't eliminate NSAID-induced ulcer risk; outright avoidance is still safest.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A patient develops headache and dizziness after a lumbar puncture. What is the most appropriate immediate nursing action?
questions.explanation: Post-LP headache is managed by keeping the patient flat (supine or prone) for several hours with fluids; reduces CSF leak symptoms.

explanations.A: The CSF sample is usually already sent; the focus now is patient comfort/safety.
explanations.B: Post-LP headache is managed by keeping the patient flat (supine or prone) for several hours with fluids; reduces CSF leak symptoms.
explanations.C: Notify after addressing positioning and fluids if pain is severe/persistent.
explanations.D: Deep breathing doesn't resolve low-pressure headache.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common side effect of nitroglycerin?
questions.explanation: Cerebral vasodilation → throbbing headache is the commonest NTG side effect.

explanations.A: Nitrates cause reflex tachycardia, not bradycardia.
explanations.B: Cerebral vasodilation → throbbing headache is the commonest NTG side effect.
explanations.C: Nausea can occur but is less frequent than headache.
explanations.D: Palpitations from reflex tachycardia are less common as a complaint than headache.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A patient is suspected of having acute pancreatitis. Which laboratory values are most commonly elevated?
questions.explanation: Serum amylase and especially lipase (>3× upper limit) are the diagnostic biomarkers of acute pancreatitis.

explanations.A: Serum amylase and especially lipase (>3× upper limit) are the diagnostic biomarkers of acute pancreatitis.
explanations.B: Triglycerides are a cause of pancreatitis but not the diagnostic marker.
explanations.C: ALT/AST rise in biliary pancreatitis but are not specific to pancreas.
explanations.D: Creatinine rises if AKI complicates severe disease but isn't primary.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A patient's ABG shows pH 7.50, PaCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3 24 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: ABG shows acute respiratory alkalosis (↑pH, ↓PaCO2, normal HCO3) — typical of PE-induced hyperventilation.

explanations.A: COPD classically produces respiratory acidosis (↑PaCO2), not alkalosis.
explanations.B: ABG shows acute respiratory alkalosis (↑pH, ↓PaCO2, normal HCO3) — typical of PE-induced hyperventilation.
explanations.C: Air embolism is rarer; PE fits the hyperventilation pattern best here.
explanations.D: Pure hypoxia may drive hyperventilation but PE is the best clinical fit.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A patient is unconscious after trauma with suspected cervical spine injury. What is the priority nursing intervention?
questions.explanation: Rigid cervical collar + manual in-line stabilisation is first to prevent secondary cord injury.

explanations.A: Airway protection is important but any manipulation must happen with the neck immobilised.
explanations.B: Circulation support follows airway/spine protection.
explanations.C: Neurological assessment is secondary; must not delay immobilisation.
explanations.D: Rigid cervical collar + manual in-line stabilisation is first to prevent secondary cord injury.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A patient with chronic kidney disease presents with hyponatremia. What is the most appropriate initial nursing intervention?
questions.explanation: In symptomatic hyponatremia with CKD, isotonic saline (0.9% NS) is the safest initial step to restore sodium gradually.

explanations.A: In symptomatic hyponatremia with CKD, isotonic saline (0.9% NS) is the safest initial step to restore sodium gradually.
explanations.B: Fluid restriction suits SIADH-type dilutional hyponatremia, not hypovolemic or CKD-related loss.
explanations.C: 3% saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatremia with neurological signs; requires close monitoring.
explanations.D: Diuretics can worsen hyponatremia in CKD.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical

questions.question: A patient with central diabetes insipidus receives vasopressin. What is the expected effect on urine?
questions.explanation: ADH concentrates urine — urine specific gravity rises toward normal.

explanations.A: Vasopressin promotes water reabsorption at the collecting duct; urine volume decreases.
explanations.B: ADH concentrates urine — urine specific gravity rises toward normal.
explanations.C: Urine volume and concentration change markedly with DDAVP in central DI.
explanations.D: Lowering specific gravity is the opposite of the expected response.

questions.subject: Fundamentals

questions.question: Patients on monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) should avoid which of the following?
questions.explanation: Tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, cured meats, soy, fermented products) cause hypertensive crisis with MAOIs.

explanations.A: Tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, cured meats, soy, fermented products) cause hypertensive crisis with MAOIs.
explanations.B: Glucose has no interaction with MAOIs.
explanations.C: Fructose has no relevant MAOI interaction.
explanations.D: Lactose has no relevant MAOI interaction.

questions.subject: Fundamentals

questions.question: A patient presents with dilated pupils, elevated blood pressure, and tachycardia. What type of pain is this?
questions.explanation: Sympathetic activation (mydriasis, ↑BP, tachycardia, diaphoresis) characterises acute pain.

explanations.A: Sympathetic activation (mydriasis, ↑BP, tachycardia, diaphoresis) characterises acute pain.
explanations.B: Chronic pain usually has parasympathetic dominance with normal vitals and depression/fatigue.
explanations.C: Neuropathic pain presents with burning/shooting sensations, less autonomic change.
explanations.D: Visceral pain has diffuse poorly localised features — autonomic signs may overlap but acute pain is the textbook answer.

questions.subject: Fundamentals

questions.question: The passage of bright red blood per rectum is referred to as:
questions.explanation: Hematochezia = fresh bright red blood PR, usually lower GI bleed.

explanations.A: Hematochezia = fresh bright red blood PR, usually lower GI bleed.
explanations.B: Melena = black tarry stool (upper GI bleed digested).
explanations.C: Hematemesis = vomiting blood.
explanations.D: Occult blood = microscopic, not visible.

questions.subject: Fundamentals

questions.question: A patient's chest tube becomes accidentally dislodged. What is the most appropriate immediate nursing action?
options: Immerse the tube end in sterile saline
questions.explanation: Cover the site with a sterile petroleum-gauze / 3-sided dressing to prevent air entry and tension pneumothorax.

explanations.A: Re-immersing a dislodged tube risks introducing contamination; the priority is sealing the wound.
explanations.B: Cover the site with a sterile petroleum-gauze / 3-sided dressing to prevent air entry and tension pneumothorax.
explanations.C: Clamping a functioning chest drain can cause tension pneumothorax.
explanations.D: Deep breathing worsens air entry through the open wound.

questions.subject: Fundamentals

questions.question: During suctioning, a patient's oxygen saturation drops from 94% to 88%. What should be the immediate nursing action?
questions.explanation: Stop suction, hyperoxygenate with 100% O2 via BMV/AMBU, allow recovery before re-suction.

explanations.A: Continuing causes further hypoxia and bradyarrhythmia.
explanations.B: Stop suction, hyperoxygenate with 100% O2 via BMV/AMBU, allow recovery before re-suction.
explanations.C: Higher suction pressure damages mucosa and doesn't address hypoxia.
explanations.D: Physician notification is secondary to immediate resuscitation.

questions.subject: Fundamentals

questions.question: The patient's urine output is 100 mL in 24 hours. How is this classified?
questions.explanation: Anuria is <100 mL/24 h — 100 mL lies at the cutoff and is labelled anuria in most Indian texts.

explanations.A: Oliguria = <400 mL/day (or <0.5 mL/kg/hr).
explanations.B: Anuria is <100 mL/24 h — 100 mL lies at the cutoff and is labelled anuria in most Indian texts.
explanations.C: Polyuria is >3 L/day.
explanations.D: Normal adult output is 1000–2000 mL/day.

questions.subject: Fundamentals

questions.question: A nurse is instructed to infuse 1000 mL of IV fluid over 8 hours using an IV set with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. What should be the correct infusion rate in drops per minute?

explanations.A: 42 is the rate for a drop factor of 20 gtt/mL (not 15).
explanations.C: 25 matches drop factor of 12.
explanations.D: 18 is less than half; incorrect arithmetic.

questions.subject: Fundamentals

questions.question: A woman undergoing evaluation for infertility is advised a hysterosalpingogram. On which day of the menstrual cycle should the nurse schedule this procedure?
questions.explanation: HSG is ideally done in the proliferative phase, days 7–10 post-menses, before ovulation. Day 8 fits.

explanations.A: Day 21 is the luteal phase — risk of early pregnancy disruption.
explanations.B: Day 14 is ovulation; radiation risk if conception has occurred.
explanations.C: Day 3 is too early; menstruation may still be occurring.
explanations.D: HSG is ideally done in the proliferative phase, days 7–10 post-menses, before ovulation. Day 8 fits.

questions.subject: OBG

questions.question: Identify the given instrument (atraumatic clamp with triangular fenestrated tips used on uterine angles).
questions.explanation: Green-Armytage forceps are used in LSCS to grasp uterine angles and control bleeding.

explanations.A: Green-Armytage forceps are used in LSCS to grasp uterine angles and control bleeding.
explanations.B: Babcock has rounded atraumatic ring tips, used for delicate tissue like appendix.
explanations.C: Allis has serrated teeth — grasping traumatic forceps.
explanations.D: Kocher's has heavy serrations and 1×2 teeth — for tough pedicles.

questions.subject: OBG

questions.question: Identify the given instrument (wide, scoop-shaped abdominal retractor).
questions.explanation: Deaver is a broad, curved right-angle retractor for deep abdominal exposure.

explanations.A: Doyen's is a curved bladder retractor used in LSCS.
explanations.B: Deaver is a broad, curved right-angle retractor for deep abdominal exposure.
explanations.C: Langenbeck is a small L-shaped retractor for superficial wounds.
explanations.D: Morris is a curved retractor with a broader blade than Langenbeck but not Deaver-shape.

questions.subject: OBG

questions.question: Identify the item shown in the image (fenestrated obstetric drape with V-shaped leg opening).
questions.explanation: V-drape isolates the perineum for vaginal delivery; V-shaped cut-out at the leg opening.

explanations.A: V-drape isolates the perineum for vaginal delivery; V-shaped cut-out at the leg opening.
explanations.B: Episiotomy packs hold instruments, not drapes.
explanations.C: Perineal sheet is a smaller under-buttock drape.
explanations.D: Cesarean drape has an abdominal fenestration, not a V leg opening.

questions.subject: OBG

questions.question: A cardiotocography tracing shows cord compression. Which fetal heart rate pattern is most expected?
questions.explanation: Cord compression produces variable decelerations (abrupt onset, variable depth/timing).

explanations.A: Cord compression produces variable decelerations (abrupt onset, variable depth/timing).
explanations.B: Late decels indicate uteroplacental insufficiency.
explanations.C: Early decels mirror contractions; caused by fetal head compression.
explanations.D: Hypoxia is an outcome, not a CTG pattern.

questions.subject: OBG

questions.question: A patient develops uterine hyperstimulation after administration of prostaglandins for induction of labour. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Terbutaline (β-agonist) is the tocolytic of choice for uterine hyperstimulation.

explanations.A: Calcium gluconate reverses MgSO4 toxicity; not used for tachysystole.
explanations.B: MgSO4 is for seizure prophylaxis in eclampsia, not tocolysis of PG-induced hyperstimulation.
explanations.C: Hydralazine is an antihypertensive.
explanations.D: Terbutaline (β-agonist) is the tocolytic of choice for uterine hyperstimulation.

questions.subject: OBG

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman has a history of 3 consecutive first-trimester abortions, no structural uterine abnormality, normal blood sugars, and is positive for antiphospholipid antibody. What is the most likely diagnosis?
